We’re Building Up a Tech Debt. Who’s Going to Pay It?

Watch now (20 mins) | Q&A with an AI expert on what to expect. Plus: The true cost of data centers. Say goodbye to America’s most notorious jail. Iowans fight a lead explosion. And solving a key vaccine problem.

We’re Building Up a Tech Debt. Who’s Going to Pay It?

Q&A with an AI expert on what to expect. Plus: The true cost of data centers. Say goodbye to America’s most notorious jail. Iowans fight a lead explosion. And solving a key vaccine problem.

Jessica Yellin and Rohan Montgomery

Nov 20

READ IN APP

For daily news, updates, and analysis, be sure to follow us on Instagram. If you are able to support independent journalism, please make a tax-deductible donation to News Not Noise here.

This week offered a clearer picture of where the AI revolution may be headed, and who’s enjoying the ride. The people in the cockpit are getting spectacularly rich. The rest of us are in coach, wondering why we’re losing altitude and whether anyone knows how to land this thing.

Anthropic went public in the largest IPO in history, while experts warned that our aging infrastructure is buckling under the strain of rapid AI adoption. Bridgewater, the hedge fund known for spotting trouble ahead, warned of an economy-crushing cyber catastrophe. And those are the mild predictions.

I know. You’d rather not think about it. Frankly, neither would I. But there’s a problem when the people paying closest attention to AI are the tech insiders building it and the investors financing it. Neither group is known for pumping the brakes.

So the rest of us had better learn what we’re flying into.

Today I spoke with Aalok Mehta, who helped shape AI policy at OpenAI and Google and now directs the AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Watch our discussion at the top of this newsletter.

Listen closely to two terms: tech debt and failure mode. They may come in handy the next time someone assures us that safety comes first and the people in charge have everything under control.

Here Are Your Headlines

Breaking: A jury convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht of starting the 2025 Palisades fire, which became one of the most destructive fires in LA history.

Slip and Slide: Anthropic’s record-setting IPO didn’t stop the market’s slide. The S&P 500 is on its longest losing streak in years and is down more than 10% from last month’s peak, officially a “correction.” The tech-heavy Nasdaq has erased all its gains for the year, and both are on track for their worst week in at least a year. Thin holiday trading may be making it worse, but many investors are increasingly worried the AI boom can’t last. Here’s the latest:

Claude’s Riches: Anthropic’s IPO raised $81.3 billion, valuing the AI developer at $1.5 trillion. The historic public offering made 96% of the young company’s staff millionaires and its seven co-founders billionaires.

The Chips are Down: Nvidia’s stock keeps tumbling as investigations pile up. California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed the company, and the SEC is reportedly investigating whether it misled investors. House Democrats are probing allegations that Nvidia persuaded the Commerce Department to drop its probe of Megaspeed, the company accused of smuggling advanced AI chips into China. Commerce’s top export-control official, Jeffrey Kessler, reportedly let Nvidia discuss the case with department officials.

Everybody Gets Chips: Commerce approved sales of hundreds of thousands of AI chips this year to Chinese companies the Pentagon says are tied to China’s military, according to a new House Foreign Affairs Committee report. One former official said the “astonishing” findings call “into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these [export] licenses.” Separately, a CNN investigation found that at least half a dozen blacklisted Chinese universities, some with military ties, bought restricted AI chips, including Nvidia’s.

Share

Meeting of Minds: Trump’s trip to China, including his unprecedented three-way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, was heavy on symbolism and light on substance. The leaders flattered each other and themselves at length but produced little more than a joint “peace declaration.” It called for: A “dialogue on reducing nuclear risks,” with no timeline; more oil supply; UN reform; and protecting state officials from international prosecution, which would benefit Putin, who faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for alleged war crimes in Ukraine. It didn’t mention any hot button issues like Ukraine, Iran, or Taiwan.

Delicate Issue: Trump reportedly didn’t raise the Jensen Huang scandal, apparently worried it would be “insulting” to China, which denies that Alice Huang spied for Beijing. Trump claimed Xi called Huang a “brilliant man,” though strangely, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Huang didn’t come up at all. Trump said Nvidia should be allowed to sell “older,” less advanced chips to China. He also said he and Xi agreed on “joint guardrails” for AI, without giving details. Separately, he rejected “globalist regulation” that might “destroy the tremendous potential” of AI, which he called “almost completely good.”

Carefully Choreographed: The summit was a major win for Xi, who cemented China’s position as a superpower, and Putin, who reemerged on the global stage after years of isolation following his invasion of Ukraine. Some experts criticized Trump’s flattery of both leaders — he called Putin “my friend” — as appeasement.

Dissonance: As Trump and Putin discussed peace, Russia launched what Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy called “one of the largest attacks” of the war, killing at least 8. Some Russian missiles landed in Poland, which Poland’s prime minister called an “intentional provocation.”

Taking Stock: Trump made hundreds of stock market trades collectively worth tens of millions of dollars in September, a CNBC analysis showed. His accounts bought millions of dollars of shares in Palantir and SpaceX shortly before the companies won major government contracts, and of Nvidia as Trump was cultivating a close relationship with then–CEO Jensen Huang and some of his administration officials were reportedly resisting pressure to restrict the company’s exports over national security concerns.

Went Down Like a Lead Balloon: A federal judge blocked the U.S. Army from detonating thousands of pounds of lead azide, a volatile compound used in detonators, stored at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. The Army warned the material had degraded so badly it couldn’t be moved or neutralized and that colder weather would raise the risk of an accidental, potentially deadly explosion. It gave Middletown residents a month’s notice, though it reportedly had concerns about the potential danger for decades. But thousands of Iowans, including some elected officials, only learned of the risk days before the planned detonation, which the Army warned would release a massive cloud of lead dust into the atmosphere. Environmental activists sued. Lead is a neurotoxin, particularly dangerous to kids and pregnant women. No amount of exposure is considered safe.

A map shared by the U.S. Army warning Iowans where they might be exposed to lead dust. The dust cloud’s size and spread depends heavily on the wind speed and direction if and when the stored lead azide is detonated (or explodes).

Alright, You Win: The DOJ abandoned its lawsuit challenging Alaska’s senate race after Democratic candidate Mary Peltola won more votes than all other candidates combined, including incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan. Catch up on that here.

No Proselytizing in the Workplace: A federal judge ruled that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins went “too far” by sending department-wide emails with explicitly religious Christmas and Easter messages. In a suit brought by employees, the judge found Rollins used her “position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion,” violating the First Amendment. The judge ordered her to follow USDA’s own guidance against pressuring subordinates.

Share

Find and Replace: Trump fired National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross, reportedly at the urging of chief of staff Stephen Miller, and replaced him with Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer. (In case you’re wondering, she joined the Pentagon after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth infamously leaked confidential battle plans on Signal.)

Disqualifying: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC) put Trump’s nomination of Michael LoSapio for director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency on hold after he refused to acknowledge that Jan 6, 2021 was an attack. LoSapio is defense contractor Palantir’s chief information security officer.

Full Steam Ahead: The Senate voted 62–33 to pass a bipartisan bill reforming environmental laws to speed up energy infrastructure projects. Critics of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act claim it will weaken environmental protections, promote fossil fuel projects, and fast-track the construction of data centers on public lands. Supporters say the bill prevents data centers from passing on increased electricity costs to ratepayers and would fast-track renewable projects hooking into the grid.

Need More Data: Rising electricity bills and emissions are driving the national backlash against data centers. A first-of-its-kind study found that America’s 403 largest data centers emit 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide a year, more than most countries, and use almost 2% of the nation’s electricity — more than NYC and LA combined. Both figures are likely undercounts. A federal estimate puts all U.S. data centers at more than double that share, and up to 12% by 2028.

Read the Room: Trump said his administration will fight “very hard for the data centers” and will try to stop U.S. companies from building them in other countries.

Most Americans aren't comfortable with data centers being in their community

Percentage of respondents who say they would be "..." comfortable with a new data center operating in their area:

New Chapter: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a plan to close Rikers Island, the city’s infamously dysfunctional and abusive jail complex, by 2032, five years after a legal deadline. The plan involves moving detainees to a new network of borough-based jails and hospitals. Mamdani promised not to “transfer the historic and endemic failures of Rikers to new locations” across the city.

News That Doesn’t Suck

Vaccines Are Cool: Around the world, vaccines are thought to have saved at least 154 million lives over the last half century. That’s six lives saved every minute, with each individual gaining an average of 66 years of full health. There’s a problem, though. Newer vaccines using mRNA technology, like the COVID vaccine, are very sensitive to temperature. They use lipid nanoparticles, tiny spheres of fat, to protect the fragile RNA and get it inside your cells. Those nanoparticles must be kept in extremely low temperatures — below -4ºF and up to -112ºF in some cases — or they degrade. To get them from the manufacturer to patients requires an elaborate network of temperature-controlled transportation and storage facilities called a “cold chain.” That cold chain doesn’t reach everywhere, though. Poorer, rural areas, including in the U.S., struggle to afford the equipment, if they even have electricity at all. Up to half of all vaccines are wasted every year due to issues with temperature control. Now researchers at MIT may have found a solution. They were trying to rework the lipid nanoparticle formula used with Moderna’s COVID vaccine to make it more resistant to heat. But they were “stuck,” one researcher said, which was “really frustrating.” A breakthrough finally came when they used a machine learning algorithm to identify formulations that might work. They used the algorithm’s predictions to run tests, fed the results back in, generated more predictions, ran more tests, and so on, for several rounds. Eventually, they came up with a formulation that was promising enough to be tested in mice. They left one sample at 98ºF for two months, and another at room temperature for an entire year. And yet, both samples produced the same immune response in mice as the original formulation. The best part is that this formulation of lipid nanoparticles can theoretically be used with any mRNA vaccine. It might even allow for entirely new vaccine delivery methods — like patches that use microscopic, dissolvable needles to release the vaccine into your bloodstream. Here’s to saving many more lives over the next half century.

The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification

Proving software correct with math has traditionally required specialist work. Now AI and Lean are helping automate the process. ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification

Proving software correct with math has traditionally required specialist work. Now AI and Lean are helping automate the process.

Richard MacManus | November 20, 2026

Read online

The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems, which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware.

With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems, there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic, Theorem, Axiom Math, and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking.

How formal verification is used in software and AI today

In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett, &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5, a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification.

Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro, Amazon’s agentic development environment.

“It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us.

Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett.

When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall?

“The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues] or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?”

&Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.”

Lean’s role in formal verification

&Truth builds on Lean, an open-source programming language and proof assistant. The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check.

Lean is a language used by frontier models to solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems. For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced what Vals believes is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines.

The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and he posted the proof in Lean.

Example of Lean code; via Lean project website

&Truth is building what it calls a “verification machine” on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language, proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements, and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.”

“What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.”

This has implications for model training too. Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models.

In an interview with Latent Space in June, Axiom CEO Carina Hong made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure.

“Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. It's about scaling brilliance. It's about super-intelligence.”

Scaling Past Informal AI - Carina Hong, Axiom Math

Axiom develops AxiomProver, an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE, its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs.

Harmonic’s Aristotle, an “automated theorem prover”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website.

Harmonic’s workflow

Cybersecurity and LLM-scaled formal verification

Given the heightened level of paranoia about cybersecurity these days — some might say in the days leading up to AGI — formal verification systems seem like they’re needed more than ever. And Barrett confirmed that cybersecurity is a key focus for &Truth.

“One really powerful use case for our technology is going through all the C code in the world, whether it be open source or closed source, and trying to ensure that it's memory safe. And then if it's not memory safe, we can point to: here's a problem with this piece of code, you need to fix it so that it's safe.”

Security is also a focus of Theorem, one of &Truth’s competitors. “Verification is the only defense that holds while adversaries scale,” Theorem states on its homepage.

Theorem’s proof-efficiency eval: “KB of machine code verified per hour on our proof-efficiency eval, by model release date, with 95% intervals.”

Theorem has also collaborated with Anthropic on this topic, resulting in a blog post entitled “LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale.”

One of the more encouraging notes in the post is that formal verification, although currently token-expensive, is starting to get more token-efficient. On a set of 36 small verification tasks, Anthropic reported that Opus 5.5 reached a 50% solve rate using about 40% fewer tokens than Opus 5. This trend is expected to continue as more models are “trained on long verification tasks.”

Theorem and Anthropic describe “LLM-scaled formal verification” as a promising approach to providing security guarantees at a previously impractical scale.

Anthropic diagram: “from code to a machine-checked guarantee”; in this case using Rocq rather than Lean.

The “veri-coding” experience for developers

Lastly, how does formal verification fit into a developer’s workflow? On its website, &Truth states that developers will move from vibe-coding to “veri-coding” — meaning the verification layer is part of the workflow.

“If you've got your verification machine connected to your agent, you can still say, ‘hey, I want you to build this,’ said Barrett. “Maybe there's a little bit of work to really nail down with the agent what the specification is of what you want to build. But then the agent can go under the hood, collaborate with the formal [verification] tool, and essentially what you'll see is almost no difference except your code will work the first time.”

The idea, then, is that more of the developer’s time will be spent on spec writing and reviewing than on coding or reviewing code.

Verify all the outcomes

While I was finishing up this article, I came across this tweet by Cognition dev rel Nader Dabit:

Whether the term “outcome engineering” sticks or not, he’s onto something in terms of where we are with coding. When you just tell your team of agents what you want and they go ahead and build it, you (the human developer) need a way to check the correctness of what your agents deliver.

If companies like &Truth, Harmonic, Theorem and Axiom Math have their way, formal verification could become an increasingly practical way to check those outcomes.

YOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB4TJvMpN4sedax_pnXcs1UkuNkHNzwRUqZtqsKIVoZtkWt28ZRS8HxNcnbQ0c0iPrainbcjUP2NOTePYkSkKv2lFiBNNd1s0m-AbLKPasg Investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major data centre project that has so far been embraced by legislators. Credit: Getty/O'Leary digital

Opposition to data centres has become a key political issue in the US, but some in Canada are seeing it as something else: an opportunity. The country hosts a fraction of these buildings compared with the US, but it is being increasingly pitched as a hub for the infrastructure powering the artificial intelligence boom.

Nadine Yousif, senior Canada reporter

What makes Canada want to embrace data centres?

Those in favour argue that the country's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, such as data centres' proximity to populated areas, noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.

Where are these data centres going to be?

Alberta is at the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom - 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built in the western province, which is rich with natural gas deposits.

Is there any sort of opposition?

There were some furious residents in attendance at recent public information sessions on plans for provincial AI data centres. In a bid to ease concerns, the Alberta government has proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built. There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.

Major Russian missile attack kills eight after Putin retaliation threat

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB36STxr8osyeRM7JLEDUp0u0EalTV0NZYXVvbfCmv7BaPSvKj0uy35S8NdIrFcPUbOohl0O04ZMx3qxrH1sWRoH-zPWSF9NyzanmfADU Air raid sirens in Kyiv lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning. Credit: Reuters

A wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine overnight hit three bridges in Kyiv. Ballistic missiles targeted vital routes over the Dnipro River, with six deaths confirmed, while in the western city of Lviv, two people were killed in an attack on a train station. BEYOND THE HEADLINES

The mission to unlock Mercury's mysteries

https://click.email.bbc.com/?qs=ABl7ImQiOjUwNjYsInQiOjYzODcsInMiOjZ9AAYAAAAAB36STxsPrUXmP_hBhENnIOL8mErzzyZ9nQcqcWOnvrk1CWfQ4TRen-QZmRwAbZWdR4iUtgqGfhhzG8zt8SHVCnylrU8BQEnD8dk7c5PW The BepiColombo mission will spend at least a year studying Mercury. Credit: Nasa

The success of an eight-year long space mission to better understand Mercury centres on a 37-minute handbrake turn a spacecraft needs to make to get it into orbit. After a journey of almost six billion miles (10bn km) that began in 2018, the Bepicolombo craft is nearing its final destination. Scientists hope the mission will shed light on why the closest planet to the Sun has ice in its polar craters, and what the strange dents covering its surface actually are.

Hey Siri, run my Mac?

Plus, bad news if you have a Visa or Mastercard.

November 20, 2026View Online | Sign Up | Shop

Presented By

Artificial’s movie poster looks like total AI slop. There’s the uncanny sheen of Andrew Garfield’s face. His eerily glowing eyes. Not to mention the cursed Where’s Waldo of strange details you can spot in the background—like a face that appears on a tree trunk, or the Golden Gate Bridge missing the part that you actually drive on. (As a bonus, zoom in on the tree branches for a minor jump scare.)

But it turns out that the “slop” was actually made from scratch, by humans, on purpose. This artwork for the upcoming Sam Altman biopic was painstakingly hand-painted—here’s a quick time-lapse of the elbow grease it took—and is a send-up of the kind of fever-dream hallucinations that ChatGPT might produce. The movie’s cheeky tagline: “What is the image of the future that you see?”

The Download

Apple finally RSVPs to the AI agent party

Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Adobe Stock

TL;DR: AI agents are the tech industry’s latest obsession, and Apple is now getting in on the game. While the company is fashionably late, its reputation for privacy could give it an edge. Whether it can deliver is another question, given Siri AI’s rocky rollout.

What happened: Apple is building a proactive, agentic AI assistant, per several job listings spotted by Bloomberg. Here’s what that means in human terms: “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” one listing reads. That includes browsing the web, writing code, using apps, and calling services for you.

Apple is eyeing a launch as soon as late next year, per Bloomberg—but it’s already playing catch-up: Meta’s Muse has held the No. 2 spot on the list of free apps in Apple’s App Store since its debut (after premiering at No. 1).

Privacy, please: Apple seems to be paying attention to the mounting concerns over AI agents’ access. In its job listings, the company says agents that can “run code, use credentials, and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models,” plus sandboxing (keeping the AI in its own fenced-off space), and transparency (whatever that means).

It’s also holding rivals’ agents to that standard already—the latest macOS beta warns users before they let outside AI agents take over their Macs, and turning on ChatGPT’s Mac controls now takes 14 whole steps, up from four. (Apple claims it’s for security; rivals say it’s attempting to slow the competition.)

Siri-ously though: Apple’s foray into AI has so far been…underwhelming. Its upgraded Siri arrived about two years behind schedule, and it’s still working out the kinks. This month, Apple opened the assistant to developers so it can take actions inside third-party apps, like changing your ride-share pickup spot. But Siri still stumbles on the basics: In a test of the Apple HomeView smart display, Siri gaslit tech journalist Joanna Stern by insisting it didn’t have a camera (it does), among other baffling blunders.

The rest of the agent world isn’t doing much better, though—Muse reportedly read a Meta employee’s encrypted Signal messages (Signal said today it will start restricting screenshots to keep agents out). According to Reuters, Muse also messaged some employees about things they never did, and announced bank balances unprompted, some of which didn’t belong to its users (it’s unclear whether they were someone else’s or completely made up).

Bottom line: Building an agent right into its devices could give Apple a leg up, as long as it learns from Siri’s growing pains. —LC

Without the right infrastructure underneath, it’s kind of a nightmare for developers + marketing leaders. One dropped call or misplaced message, and a customer’s holiday shopping experience is undone—and their attention leaves, possibly grabbed by a competitor.

When traffic peaks, Twilio still performs. Their free guide covers the six areas most likely to buckle under the holiday load and the products that strengthen each one: SendGrid for high-deliverability email, Programmable Messaging and Voice for reach, and Verify and Lookup for fraud defense.

Get AI to help you with your data review slides

If you work with data in any capacity, you know how annoying it can be to pull it all together (especially if it’s spread across multiple sheets, programs, or platforms). Even more frustrating? Presenting it in a simple, aesthetically pleasing way so others can make sense of it.

I ran into this issue after adding a quick data review session to our pitch meetings a month ago. Originally, I would open a Google doc and split view it with our analytics platform, then we’d try to match things up live to see how everything was going. As you can imagine, I began dreading those 10 minutes after just a week, because the whole thing felt tedious and mentally exhausting (especially first thing in the morning; I am not a morning person).

Thankfully, if there’s one thing AI is good for, it’s parsing through data (as long as you give it guardrails). So I spent half a day going back and forth with a chatbot to create a skill that gathers the data and puts it into slides that are easy to understand.

Here’s how to do it, in two steps:

1. Tell it what you need: Make sure you do this as precisely as possible, including what you’re trying to do, what data it should include (plus where to get it), and how you want the information presented and why. For this part, I would recommend using a more advanced model (just know it will take up more of your usage—and data stuff can already be pretty usage-intensive). Once you’ve given it the context, add this to the end of your prompt:

Is there anything else you need to know before you get started? Let’s also create a test slide so we can make changes before you pull everything together. Once I say it’s in a good place, create a skill that will do this automatically on [insert day/time].

2. Confirm and iterate: Double-check the data on the test slide against your raw data to make sure the chatbot’s doing things accurately. And if you don’t like the way it’s presenting the data, go back and forth until the slide looks good to you. Then, once it’s running the skill, don’t be afraid to adjust further if there are changes or additions you want it to make (it’ll update the skill automatically).

Bonus: Since data stuff can be really token-heavy, it’s a good idea to have your chatbot turn the conversation into a markdown file that it can refer to if you start a new conversation to make changes or ask questions about the data review (otherwise, you’ll likely burn through your usage before you can say the words “our KPIs this quarter are…”)

After a month of doing this, I can confirm it’s made a huge difference for my attitude in the morning meetings (just ask Whizy and Lindsey)—and made the data review more enjoyable for all of us. —SM

The Jensen Huang fan club is in shambles

Morning Brew Inc., Photo: Adobe Stock

It turns out that Jensanity is not, in fact, over. While Nvidia’s board seems completely uninterested in getting back together with its ex-CEO, many of Silicon Valley’s top tech bros are still ride or die for Huang. Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick declared this week that he would personally protest alongside “tons of Nvidia employees” in front of the company’s headquarters—armed with a megaphone “encrusted” in silicon wafers. (Kalanick, after all, knows a thing or two about resigning as CEO.)

Elon Musk, meanwhile, compared ousting Huang to “kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak.” And Palmer Luckey, founder of the defense tech firm Anduril, offered this 4D-chess logic for why Huang should be brought back: “China wants Jensen out, so I want him in.” (How does he know China is happy about this? Who knows.)

Currently, a “Stand with Jensen” online petition has garnered over 200,000 signatures, not only from Kalanick and Musk but also from Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. (Unsurprisingly, Huang says he’d be “honored” to get his job back.) If you’re a current tech CEO shaken by this alleged-spy situationship—or, say, an employee at an AI company that just had the biggest IPO ever—here are some practical tips for not falling for a potential foreign agent. —WK

NEWSLETTER · 20 Nov 2026, 18:27

🟡 The outage era

In this edition, why many in the tech industry think an AI downturn might be a positive development,͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌ ͏‌

November 20, 2026

Read on the web

Sign up for our free email briefings→

Tech Today

More outages are coming

The next big AI fear?

OpenAI limits access

Betting on Jensen’s future

The chatbot economy

Why the AI industry thinks a downturn won’t be that bad, and the cultural phenomenon that is GTA VI.

First Word

Anthropic’s IPO went on as well as anyone could have reasonably hoped. It was up 17% over its initial price with a valuation of about $1.3 trillion, making it the biggest debut in history. But Anthropic shares are down 11% so far today, and the rest of the market is down, too, as skepticism of the AI trade builds.

The funny thing is, there are a lot of people in the tech industry who say they would actually like to see things slow down. That’s because all of the resources are being funneled into a small group of companies building essentially the same product, leaving little room for other ideas.

The “tokenmaxxing” craze earlier this year has accelerated revenue growth at the frontier labs and hyperscalers. But if every unit of computer memory and every accelerator is concentrated among only a handful of players, innovation — and AI adoption — starts to slow down. I’ve heard this from tech companies that work with industry players but it’s also backed up by a report by Wasabi and the Centre for Economics and Business Research.

Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia is also bad news for the pro-innovation crowd. Huang was a major proponent of open-weight AI models and a healthy startup ecosystem. The open-weight models, many of them coming out of China, were helping seed wider AI adoption, and it’s likely that will slow down if Chinese entrepreneurs and tech companies can’t get their hands on enough Nvidia chips.

Another thing that could slow AI development: the number of cybersecurity worries building up at businesses around the world (more on that below). AI is helping everyone become more productive, including threat actors and nefarious nation states.

The next period could be one of massive growth for the biggest players in tech, but it’s increasingly looking like one in which the real-life impacts of AI take longer to materialize than we initially expected.

The age of outages is here

Flights grounded at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport on Nov. 13. Elijah Nouvelage/File Photo/Reuters.

It’s pretty clear now that all the recent tech outages, from the FAA’s grounding of flights to bank glitches, are the result of a wave of software updates and patches done in fear of an eventual onslaught of AI-assisted hacks. There are likely more to come, tech executives and policymakers have warned.

I see dollar signs. Everyone involved, from the hackers to the government agencies, corporations, and small businesses trying to defend themselves, is customers of the AI labs, hyperscalers, and neoclouds.

Finding and fixing vulnerabilities is among the most compute-intensive uses of AI. And the bigger bill will come when organizations begin overhauling their entire code base with memory-safe languages. Yes, in the end the internet will be more secure. But it also amounts to a massive transfer of wealth from the rest of the economy to a small number of compute providers.

“You’re only as secure as the number of tokens you spend,” Bipul Sinha, CEO of data security company Rubrik, told Semafor’s Andrew Edgecliffe-Johnson. Cybersecurity defense doesn’t increase a company’s revenue or help it roll out new products. It’s just a necessary, and hefty, cost.

— Reed Albergotti

Silicon Valley & The World • Exclusive

Is the ‘handover’ a good talking point for Silicon Valley?

Kris Tripplaar/Semafor

The tech industry has enough of a public image problem with its warnings about AI leading to human extinction, and it risks further alienating people outside of Silicon Valley if it starts popularizing “the handover.”

The handover is the period in which AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make any decisions. Sam Altman brought the idea up on stage with me this week at Silicon Valley & The World, and he believes AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a “positive” scenario, the handover turns humans into pets of AI overlords (Altman referenced Labradors): Humans have everything they need, from food to entertainment, and don’t need to work much.

The dystopian idea is mostly a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where those inside AI companies see advanced models in their raw forms, doing both scary things like breaking into the internet and amazing things like solving the world’s most difficult math theorems. There’s no evidence we’re on the verge of a handover or anything remotely like it, so tech leaders would be wise to find a more optimistic talking point.

— Reed Albergotti

OpenAI tightens grip on model resellers

OpenAI put a new rule in place that gives the company more control over how much of the world — including China — can access its AI models. Gateways and routers that provide third-party access to OpenAI’s tech now need the company’s review and approval. Such gateways, the most prominent of which is OpenRouter, have become increasingly popular with developers and companies seeking access to a wide range of AI models: Instead of individual contracts with each lab, one account with a router can let you access hundreds of models from the US, Europe, and China.

Beyond the technical details, the move has implications in the global AI race. US security agencies and companies, including Anthropic, have accused Chinese AI labs of distilling, or copying, American frontier models by routing requests through intermediaries that resell access to their models, which obscures the identity of the end user. Those cases largely involved gray-market resellers, known in China as “transfer stations,” but OpenAI’s new rule extends its oversight to any service standing between it and the people using its models.

— J.D. Capelouto

Mixed Signals

Design pioneer Kelly Wearstler thinks Instagram is flattening our taste. Wearstler, the Instagram-famous designer and business mogul, joins this week’s Mixed Signals to talk about the interior design algorithm, whether her job is getting harder due to clients having more specific visions for their spaces, and the extent to which AI has affected her work. She also gets into her growing Substack business and pokes some fun at the universal design of video podcast studios.

Listen to the latest episode of Mixed Signals now. →

Bets on Huang’s fate on prediction markets

The Jensen Huang scandal is turning into a prediction-market bonanza for some traders. There are more than 90 separate bets on Polymarket and Kalshi relating to the outcome of various elements of the Huang story and investigations.

“Will Jensen Huang be arrested” currently has $153,000 of trading volume on Polymarket. More than 13,000 people have bet on Kalshi on whether President Donald Trump will pardon Huang. And nearly a million people have bet on if, or when, Huang will testify in front of Congress.

Some people have cashed in by making big trades right before new developments. A user named paule334 made their first Polymarket trade ever on Nov. 10, betting that Jensen Huang would resign, and continued trading until the morning of Nov. 11, the day The New York Times broke the story of Huang’s second affair. The user made about $38,000. Others made windfalls by betting quickly after news breaks. Bertapotamous, another user, made nearly $100,000 on the same trade in the late afternoon of Nov. 11, minutes after The Wall Street Journal reported Huang was set to resign.

Chatbot ads are coming

Jeenah Moon/Reuters

Most of us think of chatbots like Meta’s Muse as helpful assistants to book restaurant tables and scour the internet for the best portable phone charger. But in conversations with CEOs at Silicon Valley & The World this week, it became clear that Meta and other tech companies are already monetizing these chatbots and turning them into ad-driven moneymakers akin to the early days of search advertising.

One Fortune 500 CEO told me chatbot makers like Meta are already asking big companies to pay up to ensure their brands are displayed prominently and positively in chatbot results, much like Google did with its search engine results decades ago. And Amazon’s Andy Jassy said the e-commerce giant wouldn’t open up Muse and other agents to its shopping site until the companies could find a “fair exchange of value” — corporate speak for “pay us.” Meta declined to comment.

— Shelly Banjo

For more on the economics of AI, subscribe to Semafor’s Business briefing. →

Artificial Flavor

Athit Perawongmetha/File Photo/Reuters

Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI is on track to top $3 billion in sales in its first week and has become a cultural phenomenon, with its release sparking a wave of PTO requests and dedicated company “Game Days.” But it may be the last game of its kind: “Developers face shrinking incentives to make anything like it again,” The Economist argued. Skyrocketing hardware costs and AI have upended the video game industry’s business model, triggering mass layoffs in recent years. Not everyone in the industry sees AI as a threat, though: Xbox now lets fans use AI to combine their favorite games into mashups. And most developers have turned to AI to automate rote work. At the very least, GTA VI — which Rockstar claims was built entirely without generative AI — may be one of the last blockbuster games made without it.

NEWSLETTER · 20 Nov 2026, 18:09

Security Notice from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

Latest from Carnegie

Dear Colleague,

We are writing to inform you of a recent data breach that compromised a small segment of personal contact information maintained by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. While only a small percentage of contacts were affected, we are reaching out to all contacts in our database as a precautionary measure.

What happened:

On October 28, an unauthorized party breached a third-party vendor Carnegie uses for online donations. The breach allowed the unauthorized party to gain access to some contact information from Carnegie’s donor management and email communication database. The unauthorized access ended on October 30.

What information was involved:

The information included names, email addresses, phone numbers, and, for donors, giving history. This breach did not expose full credit card information.

What we are doing:

Carnegie retained an external cybersecurity firm to ensure the unauthorized party was fully removed from our system, increased security measures across its third-party systems, and is notifying everyone whose contact information was in the impacted database, even if their data may not have been accessed. The third-party vendor that was breached has added multiple layers of security under the guidance of an external cybersecurity firm.

What you can do:

In accordance with the requirements of the European privacy law (GDPR), we can confirm that the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. Please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or text messages asking for sensitive information, passwords, or payment, including messages that appear to come from the Carnegie Endowment. Carnegie will never ask for passwords or payment details by email or text. If you’re unsure whether a message is genuine, don’t click links or reply, and contact us using the details below.

For more information:

If you have any questions, please reach out to Katelynn Vogt at privacy@ceip.org. We take the protection of your information seriously and apologize that this occurred.

Sincerely,

Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

Why No One Can Catch Nvidia

I shared a video this week about why Nvidia is so dominant in AI, and why AMD, Intel, and the other chipmakers haven’t been able to catch up. Spoiler: it’s not really about the chip.

Here's what's going on:

Right now, about four out of every five dollars spent on AI chips goes to Nvidia.

Back in 2006, when Nvidia mostly made graphics cards for gamers, it built free software called CUDA so programmers could use its chips for more than gaming. Nvidia says it didn’t make money on it for 10 years. Then AI took off, and basically all of it got written on CUDA.

Nvidia doesn’t just sell chips anymore. It sells whole racks of 72 chips wired together to act like one giant chip, and it has reportedly booked more than half of the factory line that packages these chips, so rivals can’t get enough built.

My POV: CUDA is kind of the Windows Phone story in reverse. Windows Phone was a good phone, but all the apps were already somewhere else. With AI, all the apps were already on Nvidia.

That doesn’t make Nvidia untouchable. AMD has a huge deal with OpenAI, Google and Amazon make their own chips now, and Nvidia just lost the CEO who built all of this. But to really catch up, a rival has to beat the software, the rack, and the factory line all at once. Whatever happens with Jensen, that moat is what he built.

Hit reply and let me know: do you think anyone actually catches Nvidia in the next few years?

— Matt

Anthropic Goes Public in the Biggest IPO Ever

Via CNBC

It’s official: Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut yesterday under the ticker ANT. The company priced its highly anticipated IPO at $83 per share, above its original $70–$78 range. The stock opened at $111.50, a 34% pop, before closing the day at $97.17, up 17%. Shares then fell about 9% in early trading Friday amid a broader AI sell-off.

By the numbers:

$81.3 billion raised: The largest IPO on record, surpassing SpaceX’s $75 billion offering in June.

$1.5 trillion valuation: Puts Anthropic among the world’s most valuable technology companies. By Thursday’s close, its fully diluted market cap was roughly $1.8 trillion.

$33.24 billion in revenue: Generated during the first nine months of 2026, up approximately 1,206% year over year.

The Claude Code effect: Enterprise adoption and demand for Claude Code have fueled much of Anthropic’s explosive growth. The company has rapidly evolved from a frontier AI research lab into a major enterprise software business, although its massive computing costs remain a significant consideration for investors.

An interesting moment to go public: The debut arrives shortly after midterm elections highlighted growing public resistance to AI data centers, while Nvidia’s leadership turmoil has added uncertainty to the industry. Despite these headwinds, investors are still showing a huge appetite for a company whose fortunes are tied almost entirely to AI.

Why it matters: This is the first major test of whether public investors are willing to place trillion-dollar bets on a pure-play AI company. Anthropic’s revenue growth is staggering, but so are the infrastructure investments required to sustain it. The IPO could set the tone for how Wall Street values the next generation of AI companies, including OpenAI. Now comes the harder part: proving those valuations can hold up in public markets.

Nadella Warns America’s Infrastructure Is Unpatchable

Via CNBC

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that much of America’s critical infrastructure runs on software that can’t easily be patched, leaving essential systems increasingly vulnerable as bad actors use AI to accelerate cyberattacks.

The problem: At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit this week, Nadella pointed to internet-connected equipment like data center chillers, HVAC systems, and transportation infrastructure that rely on outdated or difficult-to-update firmware. These systems weren’t necessarily designed with modern cybersecurity threats in mind, yet many are now connected to networks that attackers can potentially reach.

AI changes the timeline: AI tools are becoming remarkably effective at discovering software vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to identify and exploit weaknesses much faster than before. Defenders often push patches directly into live systems, which can introduce unexpected failures and service disruptions.

The outage warning: Nadella also apologized for last week’s nearly daylong Outlook outage, attributing it to a “latent bug.” He said Microsoft would use lessons from the incident to improve its systems, while acknowledging that faster patching could create more instability across the industry.

Why it matters: AI is making sophisticated cyberattacks cheaper, faster, and more accessible. But simply patching vulnerabilities comes with its own set of problems. Organizations will need to modernize aging systems and develop better real-time defenses before the technology helping them find security problems faster creates even more disruption.

Your Next Video Needs a Crew. Here’s Yours.

Editors' Choice: Brits are back in Brussels

The Friday edition of our PM newsletter looks at the week that was in European politics

VIEW IN BROWSER

By Bruno Waterfield

Supported by

Hello, and welcome to Editors' Choice. I am Bruno Waterfield, Rapporteur's politics editor.

The British are back in Brussels, as we saw today when most of Andy Burnham’s cabinet decamped to the capital of the EU for a summit.

It was not quite the leaders summit of yesteryear. The British prime minister was not among true equals. He was sitting at a lesser summit table with the EU’s top officials rather than heads of state and government.

But one EU truth for British leaders trying to get the most out of a Brussels trip remains eternal (even for Burnham, whom Brussels is assiduously courting) and that is the risk of political ambush.

Accompanied with his secretaries of state, Burnham had hoped for the warm glow of an easy deal on carbon emissions alignment, less friction for food trade and a youth mobility scheme.

That was the plan, anyway. His famous smile was through gritted teeth.

As he discovered – thanks to the EU’s mulish ambassadors – nothing is ever simple and an ambush is always around the corner. My colleague Nicoletta Ionta on Rapporteur AM broke the story.

At this summit it was equal treatment on university tuition fees for European students. At the last one in May 2025, his predecessor Keir Starmer was ambushed too, on fish. Next year, he will have a “brainstorming” summit on the future with the EU. What could go wrong?

David Cameron, the former British prime minister, who lost the Brexit referendum, often complained about being hit by an unexpected or unpleasant surprise in Brussels conjured up by the fiendish Europeans.

Caught off his crease after a 2013 EU budget debate, a visibly seething Cameron said that prime ministers at a Brussels summit needed a loaded gun, a chambered round and to be ready to fire. “In this town you have to be ready for an ambush at any time, and that means lock and load and have one up the spout, and be ready for it,” he said.

Sage advice for Burnham.

Visit Rapporteur

Supported by Tyres Europe

Tyres are critical to everyday Europe

Ambulances, buses, delivery trucks and tractors all depend on a reliable supply of tyres. An Oxford Economics study shows what EU tyre manufacturing means for Europe’s economy. Learn more here.

Across the policy desks

Energy, Environment and Transport

Methane rules: Much as we would have liked to bring you news of a breakthrough by EU negotiators at the COP31 summit in Antalya (talks look set to drag on into the weekend), the main European climate policy news this week was on the other side of the carbon balance sheet. While Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra battles to keep mitigation alive in Turkey, MEPs and governments agreed in Brussels to postpone a crackdown on methane emissions by two years. Though CO2 gets most of the blame, CH4 is actually responsible for a third of global warming. And because it is far more potent but relatively short-lived, any reduction in emissions would mean a disproportionately beneficial attenuation of the greenhouse effect.

– Robert Hodgson

Technology

TikTok’s ‘rabbit holes’: The tech desk’s Anupriya Datta reports this week on new research into TikTok that found the platform fed high risk content to test accounts configured as young teenagers within minutes of them joining the service. Salvatore Romano from global non-profit AI Forensics told Rapporteur that so-called “rabbit hole effects” – whereby TikTok’s personalised feeds send users to dark places – is a “long-standing issue” with the app. While TikTok rejects criticisms that its platform is unsafe, evidence is mounting.

– Natasha Lomas

Defence

European armies test Ukraine war lessons. The Koalicja multinational military exercise in Poland has exposed language barriers and highlighted the challenges European forces face adapting to modern warfare. The Multinational Force for Ukraine drilled cooperation across land, sea and air with troops also running through measures to protect themselves from terrorism, hybrid threats and drone attacks – the main threats they expect to face if deployed after a ceasefire in the country.

– Alice Tidey

Health

Ashes for ashes: French activists threw ashes at Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi as he delivered a speech at the European Cancer Summit this week – which he nonetheless finished, despite the disruption. Our reporter Océane Duboust was at the scene and spoke with the activists from the collective Cancer Colère. “We’re here to show that people are dying of cancer today, we’re also speaking out against the fact that there are people making a fortune off our deaths,” a Cancer Colère member said.

– Brenda Strohmaier

Agrifood

CAP in transition. Parliament negotiators on the post-2027 Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) fear that farmers will have little time to prepare for the new rules, and are calling on the Commission to propose transition measures. The Lithuanian presidency says it is ready to work on one if needed, as Maria Simon Arboleas reports. The Commission remains resistant, but precedent is not on its side.

– Angelo Di Mambro

Franziska Nocke und das Playbook Team nehmen Sie jeden Morgen mit ins Regierungsviertel. Von FRANZISKA NOCKE Schicken Sie uns Tipps hier und hier | Da

Franziska Nocke und das Playbook Team nehmen Sie jeden Morgen mit ins Regierungsviertel.

Von FRANZISKA NOCKE

Schicken Sie uns Tipps hier und hier | Das Playbook anhören oder online lesen

Guten Tag! Hier meldet sich Franziska Nocke. In der Diplomatie gilt eine ungeschriebene Faustregel: Wer den Ort bestimmt, bestimmt auch die Bedingungen. Nach Shenzhen, wo Trump, Xi und Putin ohne Europa am Tisch saßen, kommt jetzt die Einladung aus dem Kreml. Reden wollen auch die Europäer. Die Frage ist nur: wo?

In 200 Sekunden sprechen wir mit Sebastian Fiedler über teure Ruanda-Pläne für 40 Fälle, mit Philipp Rottwilm über Privatjet-Steuern, mit Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann über „Alphamännchen“ und ihr vielsagendes Schweigen zur Ukraine, mit Roderich Kiesewetter darüber, wie aus Willigen endlich Entschlossene werden — und mit Luis Bobga über Gen-Z-Frust.

Von Minsk bis zur Arktis: Morgen spricht Gordon Repinski mit der belarussischen Bürgerrechtlerin Swetlana Tichanowskaja. Am Sonntag diskutiert Rixa Fürsen im Security Sunday mit Robert Habeck darüber, warum Grönland und die Arktis für Donald Trump so wichtig werden.

THEMA DER WOCHE

VIEL BILD, WENIG JALTA: Shenzhen war „vor allem ein Bildtermin“, sagt der Kanzler. Nachwirken wird vor allem Trumps Anruf aus der Air Force One. Putin wolle Frieden, ließ er die Willigen wissen, und die Ukraine-Milliarden seien anderswo besser angelegt. Was das für Europas nächste Schritte bedeutet, ordnet der heutige Playbook-Podcast ein.

Zwischen den Stühlen: Jared Kushner verkündet, Moskau akzeptiere Sicherheitsgarantien nach dem Prinzip von Artikel 5. Wolodymyr Selenskyj ist sich da „nicht sicher“. Was das Schattenspiel zwischen Shenzhen und Kanzleramt für den Westen bedeutet, analysiert Annett Meiritz.

Reden ja, Moskau nein: Boris Pistorius hält es für das falsche Signal, Putins Gesprächsangebot auszuschlagen. Als Ort komme Moskau aber nicht infrage. Welches Signal die Willigen parallel in Richtung Kreml vorbereiten, weiß Hans von der Burchard.

Wer den großen Überblick will, schaltet hier ein. Sicherheitsexpertin Claudia Major erklärt, warum Russland keinen Grund zum Kompromiss sieht und was die Ukraine durch den Winter bringt.

DAS SAGT BERLIN

DIE UNGEKRÖNTE: Hubertus Heil will für den SPD-Vorsitz kandidieren, Lars Klingbeil lässt seine Zukunft offen, und Manuela Schwesig taktiert. Warum sie zögert und was das für Klingbeil heißt, analysiert Rasmus Buchsteiner. Heil will als Parteichef kein Ministeramt. Was hieße eine SPD-Spitze ohne Regierungsamt für den Kanzler?

Nach der Sondersitzung des Präsidiums sortieren Philippa Vögeding und Maximilian Heimerzheim in der dritten Folge von Inside Links das Ergebnis und erklären, was es für Schwarz-Rot bedeutet.

SCHWACHSTROM: Acht Stunden Koalitionsausschuss, am Ende steht die Stromsteuersenkung, doch die Entlastung bleibt mager. Ob Merz nachts wirklich wutentbrannt den Raum verließ und warum das Paket 2027 schon wieder kollabieren könnte, rekonstruiert Rasmus hier. Wie es zum Milliardenpoker um Dienstwagenprivileg und Rente kam, gibt es hier.

HÖCKES RECHENWEG: Am Volkstrauertag präsentiert Björn Höcke stark überhöhte deutsche Opferzahlen. Bei Inside AfD zerlegen Pauline von Pezold und Frederik Schindler, wie diese Umdeutung funktioniert und auf welche fragwürdigen Quellen sie sich stützt.

WELTMEISTER IM ABSEITS: Mit Thomas Berthold nominiert die AfD einen Bundespräsidentschaftskandidaten, der Verschwörungserzählungen und Reichsbürger-Thesen verbreitet. Am 30. Januar tritt er gegen Ilse Aigner an. Chancenlos, aber nicht folgenlos?

AROUND THE WORLD

DIE UMSETZER: So nennen sich die fünf EU-Staate, die abgelehnte Asylbewerber ab 2027 nach Ruanda bringen wollen. Für Deutschland sind laut Sebastian Fiedler gerade einmal 40 Plätze vorgesehen. Ob das Modell trägt, an dem schon Großbritannien gescheitert ist?

UNTERM RADAR

ENTWICKLUNG STATT EINSATZ: Bundeswehr und US-Truppen sind raus aus dem Irak, jetzt soll in Erbil die Wirtschaft übernehmen. Wie fragil das Machtvakuum zwischen IS-Überresten und pro-iranischen Milizen ist, berichtet Carlotta Diederich von vor Ort.

HINTER DEM MIC

Danke an Jonas Bartsch, Rixa Fürsen, Lorenz Lanig, Ferenc Reinke, Gordon Repinski und Maximilian Stascheit.

Feedback? Schreiben Sie mir gern.

Schönes Wochenende — wir hören uns!

NEWSLETTER · 20 Nov 2026, 17:30

From Despair to Hope in Africa

And more from The World This Week.

November 20, 2026

By Michael Froman

President, Council on Foreign Relations

Writing from Nairobi, Kenya

Editor’s note: We’ll be off for the Thanksgiving holiday next week and back on Friday, December 4.

NAIROBI, Kenya — While much of the world’s attention has pivoted to Asia this week, I thought I’d write on an oft-overlooked part of the world: Africa.

We are just wrapping up a weeklong CFR fact-finding mission to Kenya and Ethiopia. For those who have spent substantial time in Africa, it will come as no surprise that contradictions abound. In Kenya alone, we witnessed the deprivation of Kakuma, a refugee camp of more than three hundred thousand refugees, as well as the buzz of the high-tech start-up community of Nairobi. Desperation and hope live in close proximity, or even in the same place, like Kibera, the largest slum in Africa, where a grassroots community organization, Shining Hope for Communities (SHOFCO), is effecting real change.

Kakuma draws refugees largely from South Sudan and Sudan but includes families from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Uganda, and a range of other countries such as Afghanistan and Yemen. It embodies all of the challenges—and a few of the opportunities—associated with humanitarian assistance. Some refugees have been there as long as thirty years. Only eight hundred returned to their countries of origin last year. These aren’t temporary camps; they are more akin to informal settlements, quasi-cities, supported by the Kenyan government and an alphabet soup of UN agencies, government assistance programs, and international nongovernmental organizations.

When the refugees arrive, they go to a processing center. In theory, they are supposed to be there for three days and then moved to housing in the camp itself, but given a backlog caused by increased arrivals and reduced resources, some might remain in processing for as long as three years. The World Food Program (WFP) and others provide for their basic nutritional needs by serving the same meal—rice and beans—twice a day. The most vulnerable get 60 percent of the 2,100 calories considered to be the minimum daily nutritional requirement. The less vulnerable get 40 percent. When families are transferred to the camp itself, they get a ten-by-ten-foot living space which was designed to house five people but is now expected to accommodate as many as ten.

Malnutrition is a chronic issue. A visit this week to the main hospital, supported by the International Rescue Committee (IRC) found benches and benches of people waiting to be seen by the emergency room. The maternity ward is a single open room with forty patients lined up, side by side. The pediatric wing is mostly focused on stabilizing children suffering from serious malnutrition, with special high-nutrition formula and Plumpy’Nut, a peanut butter–like nutritional supplement. Chillingly, there is a chart on the wall, tracking weekly morbidity and mortality metrics. Last week, 8.7 percent of the children treated in that ward died.

And still, in the midst of all this suffering, there are rays of hope. The dirt roads among the makeshift structures are replete with small stands selling pots and pans, shoes and clothing, and tomatoes. Western Union and M-Pesa, a Kenya-based telecom payment service, facilitate remittances into the camp from relatives abroad and from refugees to their families back in South Sudan or elsewhere. The WFP and other institutions have set up a farm where five hundred refugees are being trained in farming and where whatever few vegetables are available in the camp are grown.

And then there are the stories of remarkable individuals. Take Dr. Bul, a refugee from South Sudan who came to the camp as a child, was educated in camp schools, received a scholarship to medical school in Nairobi, and now works back at the clinic in Kakuma as one of the six doctors on staff seeing an average of five hundred patients a day. And there is Fabiola, a dynamic young woman in her thirties, who turned her concern about her own children’s malnutrition into an agribusiness, the Fabiola Amazing Food Company, which now employs twenty women and produces high nutrition flour and other grain products. She received training under a WFP/Mastercard Foundation program and sells her products across Kenya.

Much of the discussion during our meetings focused on the abrupt change in U.S. foreign assistance policy in 2025 and the reduction of aid more generally by donors from other countries. There was a moment of panic after the Trump administration announced a cease-work order for U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) contractors. The staff of the pediatric wing we visited thought they would have to close, causing dozens of children to die in a short period of time. In the end, the Trump administration exempted life-saving activity, and the international organizations shifted resources to priority activities to avoid a calamity. Still, the impact of the cuts is evident everywhere, from the reduction in calories provided to the malnourished to the backlog in processing and the overcrowding of shelters. The WFP estimates that, on the current trajectory, it will run out of food to distribute in Kakuma in the spring. Resources were top of mind for everyone we met.

But it is not just an issue of money. The refugee crisis existed long before the Trump administration, and the issues raised by the administration about foreign assistance have as well: creating sustainability vs. deepening dependency, focusing on local priorities vs. congressional earmarks, investing in systemic improvements (e.g., strengthening health systems) vs. individual projects, strengthening government capacity vs. investing in parallel systems. These are all issues development experts have raised over the years as they criticized traditional approaches to foreign assistance. That said, it would be easier to address those issues in the absence of the kind of cuts that cause or exacerbate real, immediate humanitarian crises.

When it comes to development, sustainable economic growth is ultimately going to be driven by leveraging private-sector activity. The U.S. government has a number of tools to catalyze and leverage that activity. The U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) was substantially boosted by former President Joe Biden and further empowered by President Donald Trump. The Export-Import Bank, Millennium Challenge Corporation, and Trade and Development Agency all have a role to play. Loans, loan guarantees, and political risk insurance can help mitigate risk. Congress created a capacity for the DFC to provide equity financing, but government accounting rules make it cumbersome to use. That should be fixed.

Of course, some sectors, such as energy, are more attractive to private investment than others (e.g., education). The Delta 40 venture studio in Nairobi has served as an inspiring hub for entrepreneurs launching technology, fintech, and alternative energy start-ups since 2021. It would feel right at home in the Bay Area or Austin, and may well attract market-based risk capital. There is still an important role for grant funding and philanthropy, but much remains to be explored in terms of real public-private partnership.

Take agriculture: 30 percent of Kenya’s GDP is agriculture, 70 percent of the Kenyan population is involved in agriculture, and 60 percent of young people outside Nairobi are unemployed. Kenya is unlikely to meet its economic potential without its agricultural sector playing a significant role.

We visited the facilities of Kentegra, a company in the Rift Valley that is producing organic insecticides from locally grown flowers. Kentegra is making it possible for fifteen thousand farmers to make a decent living, with substantial potential upside. It has benefitted from USAID grants and DFC loans, which together reduced its risk profile and laid the groundwork for private investment that is allowing it to expand and scale. It now awaits approval by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to gain access to the U.S. market. If successful, it could be a model for development going forward because Kenya needs firms that can support tens of thousands of jobs, not just tens of jobs. The same is true across much of Africa, where the population is expected to reach 3.8 billion people by century’s end, accentuated by a huge youth bulge in the coming decades.

One thing is clear. There needs to be better linkage between humanitarian and development strategies, programs, and resources. It is inconceivable that generations could be born, live, and die in refugee camps such as Kakuma, wholly dependent on humanitarian assistance, rather than be channeled into productive activity and integrated into the broader economy. Kenya is beginning down that road with the Shirika Plan, under which camps would become municipalities and refugees would integrate further into their host communities. Given the scale of that challenge—there are more than eight hundred thousand refugees in Kenya alone, but there are more than forty million refugees and more than one hundred million forcibly displaced people (including internally displaced people) worldwide—it is going to require the kind of growth that comes from private-sector activity. And that is only going to happen if the government uses the tools at its disposal to crowd in private investment.

The cuts in assistance created crises with real human consequences, and the need to reform and improve the effectiveness of U.S. development and humanitarian policy remains. Every crisis creates opportunities. It’s important we not let this crisis go to waste.

Let me know what you think about the future of U.S. development policy and what this column should cover next by replying to president@cfr.org.

Middle Power Ties in the Gulf and Africa

The Iran War Inflection Point

By Will Todman, Aaron Stanley, Josiane Atallah, and Catherine Nzuki

Deepening Gulf-African partnerships offer investment, resilience, and greater strategic flexibility. Gulf states gain access to fast-growing markets, strategic resources, labor, food supplies, and alternative shipping networks, while African powers gain new sources of capital and greater bargaining power among competing external partners, but the durability of this relationship will depend on African states’ ability to navigate competing Gulf interests without becoming entangled in regional conflicts.

This brief by the CSIS Africa Program and CSIS Middle East Program examines relations between three key Gulf middle powers—Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar—and three key African middle powers—Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia.

The Issue

The war in Iran is pushing Gulf and African middle powers closer together. Gulf states hit by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz are turning to Africa for food security, ports, and alternative trade routes, while Africa's middle powers are seizing on the war in Iran to gain leverage, with Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia courting Gulf capital to diversify away from U.S. and Chinese investment.

• Middle powers in Africa and the Gulf have expanded their ties over the past decade, leveraging new relationships to

advance economic, political, and security interests.

• The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has the deepest ties with African middle powers, followed by Saudi Arabia. Qatar has relatively shallow ties and lacks the influence of its Gulf neighbors.

• Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia have actively increased engagement with Gulf countries, widening their partnerships and options even as they remain more economically dependent on their Gulf partners than those partners are on them.

• Previous geopolitical shocks prompted African and Gulf powers to deepen their relationships to build resilience, and current evidence suggests the war with Iran is accelerating this trend, although heightened cross-regional tensions also remain possible.

• Until now, African middle powers have balanced their ties with key Gulf states. However, increasing intra-Gulf rivalry

and regional security concerns may pressure African middle powers to choose sides

Read on CSIS.org

Iran War's Impact on Africa

Less than two weeks into the war with Iran, the Nigerian government sensed an opportunity. On March 11, 2026, then–Minister of Foreign Affairs Yusuf Tuggar appealed to Arab Gulf states to invest in Nigeria’s energy sector, casting Nigeria not as a rival hydrocarbon producer but as a partner that could help them diversify markets and build resilience. Just two months earlier, the UAE and Nigeria had signed a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA), signaling their intention to deepen trade and investment ties and expand economic cooperation across a range of sectors.

These developments show how the war with Iran has created an opportunity for middle powers in the Gulf and Africa to build on relationships they have steadily developed in order to achieve greater strategic gains. “Middle powers” possess significant economic, diplomatic, demographic, or technological weight but lack the military capabilities of superpowers to project global dominance. They exhibit a growing desire and capacity to shape events within their regions while also balancing and at times limiting the ambitions of outside powers. Many middle and emerging powers are refusing bloc alignment and using this ambiguity as leverage against great powers while continuing to hedge by forging new ties. These countries often seek to exploit geopolitical openings to influence the international system. As the global order shifts toward multipolarity and creates opportunities for middle powers to assert greater agency, states in Africa and the Gulf have worked to diversify their international ties.

This brief examines relations between three key Gulf middle powers—Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar—and three key African middle powers—Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia. These countries pursue distinct strategies. However, overall, Gulf powers leverage their partnerships with African powers to strengthen economic resilience by advancing economic diversification. The UAE has the most developed ties, Saudi Arabia is expanding its ties, and Qatar has smaller and more targeted ties to African middle powers. For their part, Nigeria, Kenya, and Ethiopia have actively increased engagement with Gulf countries to attract investment and diversify their partnerships and options, even as they remain far more economically dependent on their Gulf partners than those partners are on them.

Recent opportunities to assert agency and further diversify international relationships build on more than a decade of deeper economic engagement that is spreading into security and political spheres. As Gulf-African partnerships grow, they at times complement and at times compete with ties to great powers, including the United States and China. The war with Iran demonstrates both the opportunities and potential fragility of the expanded relationships between the two regions. It has validated strategies of diversifying ties but also caused disruptions and new uncertainty. As the war continues without a clear resolution, diversifying the economic, political, and security relationships between African and Gulf countries offers opportunities to build strategic resilience. However, it also risks the spillover of regional contests and conflict. In particular, the UAE’s and Saudi Arabia’s entanglement in conflicts in the Horn of Africa, as well as bilateral competition between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, complicates relations with African middle powers.
