The MAGA Crackup Around the Corner

Trump’s warring factions are tired of waiting for him to pick a side.

Andrew Egger, Jim Swift

READ TO ME

Hey, look: The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act last night, a badly needed piece of energy-infrastructure permitting reform. We’ll see how it does in the House, but the affordability agenda is off to a good start. Happy Friday.

(Photo illustration by Sarah Rogers/The Bulwark | Photos: Getty, Shutterstock)

The Worst Is Yet to Come

by Andrew Egger

When Trump first swept into office last year, bringing a rogues’ gallery of wacky and alarming nominees with him, the Republican Senate barely put up a fight. Pete Hegseth, Kash Patel, Kristi Noem, Tulsi Gabbard, Pam Bondi, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: Yeah, sure, fine, okay, whatever, if you insist.

But today, a Trump nominee is liable to flame out without warning. This week, the Senate effectively killed the nomination of administration lawyer T. Elliott Gaiser to a judgeship in Texas thanks to opposition from outgoing Texas Sen. John Cornyn, who seemed upset that Trump hadn’t nominated a Texas prosecutor he would have preferred.¹ And last night, Politico reported that outgoing North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis will block Tump’s nomination of White House staffer Eric Ueland to lead the Government Accountability Office.

With just weeks left of the Republican trifecta, any nominee who goes down now is unlikely to see a replacement before the lame-duck Congress leaves office—which means each failure hands more future confirmation power to incoming Senate Democrats. It’s a powerful illustration of how the various tensions and cracks in the GOP are already costing the party real power.

And these coalition splinters are only going to get worse.

Earlier this week, we briefly mentioned Dr. Heidi Overton, whom Trump nominated for commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration back in August. Trump withdrew Overton’s nomination this week, acknowledging that there was seemingly no path to confirming her and apparently resigning himself to finishing his second term without a Senate-confirmed appointee in the crucial position.

Trump will eventually go, but our troubles will remain. Join our pro-democracy community, because we’re not going anywhere.

Join

Last year, it was rare to see a figure like Overton go down without even a vote. Her MAGA credentials are strong: She’s a longtime Trump health-policy official who worked on health care issues at the America First Policy Institute during the president’s interregnum and has spent the last two years in a key role on the White House Domestic Policy Council. As tensions between MAGA and MAHA grew over the last year, Overton was as much of an internal peacemaker as any—crucial in mediating fights between HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, the Atlantic reported over the summer.

If Trump’s coalition were still basically holding together, someone like Overton—with one foot on both sides of a key internal divide—would be well positioned to thrive. But as fault lines broaden, trying to straddle them becomes more dangerous. In the end, rather than uniting warring constituencies, Overton was pulled apart by them: The MAHA faithful mistrusted her as “controlled opposition” who would work to neuter RFK Jr.’s agenda from the inside, while MAHA skeptics like Sen. Bill Cassidy worried she would work to further Kennedy’s plans to disrupt childhood vaccines.

And Overton was also caught up in another serious internal divide that hasn’t been talked about much—but which is liable to explode into yet another coalition-shaking controversy for Trump in 2027: how the FDA will handle a crucial decision on abortion policy.

During his first term, Trump saw anti-abortion activists as a key political constituency and worked hard to earn their support, appointing the judges who would overturn Roe v. Wade and embracing the label of “the most pro-life president in history.” Since his 2024 campaign, however, Trump has swerved hard to the center on the issue. He outflanked Ron DeSantis to the left during the 2024 primary, attacking Florida’s abortion laws as too restrictive. And he has pursued an essentially abortion-agnostic policy program since retaking office.

Pro-lifers have grudgingly put up with this for a few reasons. In part it’s because they remain grateful to Trump for bringing about the end of Roe. In part it’s because they recognize that the hard, broad turn of public opinion in favor of abortion access has weakened their position in the GOP coalition. And in part it’s because they are waiting to see what Trump’s FDA will do about the sale of the abortion drug mifepristone by mail, which has become one of the most salient policy issues within the larger abortion battle over the last few years. This would not require legislation: Trump’s FDA could dramatically reduce American women’s access to telehealth mifepristone by a change in regulations alone.

Back in 2024, Trump told Time Magazine it was “very unlikely” he would move to restrict the abortion drug. But as president, he’s tried to maintain a posture of maximum ambiguity, with his administration insisting it can’t rule one way or the other until the FDA completes an ongoing safety reassessment of mifepristone. Now the act is getting old. Pro-lifers are tired of waiting: Cassidy suggested that pro-life senators had been holding out on Overton’s nomination because they are demanding assurances that the next FDA commissioner will move forward quickly on this issue.

Whichever way the FDA rules spells further danger for Trump and his coalition. After two cycles where abortion politics proved highly favorable for Democrats, the issue all but dropped out of voters’ minds in 2026. But a crackdown on mifepristone would bring it back into the spotlight—while a failure to crack down could prove the final straw for a diminished but highly loyal faction of single-issue Trump voters. Overton lost her nomination fight in part because of this undodgeable dilemma. She won’t be its last casualty.

QUICK HITS

ADMITTING DEFEAT: While Donald Trump keeps impotently whining about the supposedly rigged election, the official 2026 Stop the Steal effort is dying a speedy death. Yesterday, the Trump administration dropped its legal attempt to block Democrat Mary Peltola’s victory in the Alaska Senate race, which had been predicated on the presence of two men named “Dan Sullivan” on the ballot: one the incumbent Republican senator, the other a man whom Peltola’s campaign reportedly helped recruit to siphon votes away from the other.

Administration attorneys had asked a federal court in Alaska to segregate out the sliver of ballots cast for Fake Dan during the counting process—presumably so they could be matched to voters who could then be asked whether they had intended to vote for their current senator. The court denied this request, and counting proceeded as normal. Later, the court threw out the suit altogether for lack of standing. In a filing yesterday, the administration argued that it thus had become impossible to determine whether voters had been confused enough to affect the outcome of the election, and that a higher judge should thus rule the case moot.

It had become moot for another reason too: Peltola ended up with an absolute majority of the four-candidate vote, meaning that even taking Fake Dan’s entire reservoir of votes and depositing it in Real Dan’s account wouldn’t have been enough to carry the incumbent to victory. Because the real objective for Trump was always to stop Peltola’s victory rather than to bring to light some nefarious corruption, the lawsuit became meaningless at that juncture.

GET USED TO IT: Why is all our tech suddenly going offline? Politico dives into what’s looking unfortunately like our “new normal”:

Artificial intelligence is making it easier to find software flaws that leave critical systems exposed—leading security experts to warn that mass outages will soon become standard.

“We are just at the beginning of this moment,” said Helmut Reisinger, European chief executive of cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks, referring to the accelerating pace of vulnerability discoveries and the resulting outages as the “new norm.”

The good news is that we haven’t seen any face-meltingly awful security breaches amid this maelstrom of update chaos, at least not yet. Still, plenty of systems are still limping along below full capacity—the National Security Agency, for instance, is still staggering arrival times at its Maryland headquarters to reduce the strain on its classified communications networks—and we’re still only at the dawn of this insane new era.

MONEY MONEY MONEY: The best thing to be in today’s economy is the president’s son, but being his former body man isn’t a half-bad way to make a living either. The Washington Post reports that longtime Trump aide Jason Miller made a remarkable $15 million in fiscal year 2026: “In that time, Miller was a registered foreign agent for the governments of India and Romania and was in talks to join Trump’s White House as an unpaid adviser and began appearing there regularly this summer.”

Even more remarkably, none of that money ever appeared in public disclosures. We know about it only because Miller’s finances were subpoenaed in a child-support fight with another former Trump aide, A.J. Delgado, with whom he had an affair in 2017.

Since Trump retook office, WaPo reports, Miller has inhabited a very lucrative halfway space in the administration:

Had Miller become a special government employee, he would have been exempt from federal limits on outside income and employment that apply to most White House staff, according to the Office of Government Ethics. But conflict-of-interest law would have barred him from working on government matters affecting his own financial interests or those of his clients, unless he received a waiver, said Kathleen Clark, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis who studies government ethics.

She said his lack of official status meant he could operate without committing to follow rules. “What you are describing is someone who has not sworn allegiance to this country, who doesn’t even purport to act in the interest in the public and is allowed to go running roughshod around the White House,” she said.

Embarassing and Inconsequential

Trump has himself photographed next to thugs

Anne Applebaum

Nov 20

READ IN APP

History does repeat itself—the first time as tragedy, the second time as farce.

It’s a very old formulation, but it gets repeated because it is true. While Putin ramps up ballistic missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities, while Xi steals American technology with the connivance of the Trump administration, the American president allows himself to be featured at the center of a Chinese propaganda campaign featuring all three of them. Nothing substantial was decided, no decisions were taken, there is no relief for the Ukrainians, only puffery and flattery.

From my article in The Atlantic:

The original Yalta summit took place in a rickety czarist palace on the Crimean Peninsula in February of 1945. Adolf Hitler’s troops were already in retreat when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin met in cold, drafty rooms to discuss the end of the war. Senior generals and presidential aides slept on mattresses stuffed with bedbugs. Churchill complained that Yalta was good for nothing except the “typhus and deadly lice which thrive in those parts.” Afterward, he asked for his clothes to be fumigated.

Eight decades later, the Yalta summit is remembered mostly not for building peace, but for consigning Eastern Europeans, whose leaders were not in the room, to Soviet occupation and repression for the subsequent half century. In the name of ending a war against fascist totalitarianism, in other words, Yalta promoted the spread of communist totalitarianism and planted the seeds of the Cold War.

The inconsequential Trump-Putin-Xi summit in Shenzhen, pumped up by the gullible as a “Yalta 2.0,” was an event more suited for our sillier times. No serious agreements were signed. No country’s borders were redrawn on the edge of a paper napkin. No one was infected by lice or bitten by bedbugs. Instead, the meeting was brief, almost substance-free, and carefully choreographed for the maximum benefit of the Chinese hosts. Its true purpose was not to end any wars—and certainly not to end Russia’s bloody invasion of Ukraine—but to produce propaganda photographs and video clips that each of the three leaders will now use to mask their political failures.

Certainly this was President Trump’s main goal. Before the three leaders met, he actually told Fox News that the most significant moment was already over: “the greeting yesterday, which in the history of China has never happened.” Xi Jinping, aware of how easy it is to manipulate the American president, had met Trump at his airplane, on the tarmac. “This is a highly respected, this is a great president, one of the great presidents of China—and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump blustered. He also spoke of “the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing,” adding, “That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China too.” The White House published a video clip, seemingly created to promote Chinese Communism, showing all of that fanfare and putting Trump at the center of it—a big win for China indeed, and maybe a big win for Trump’s post-midterm ego, although hardly a big win for the United States.

For Vladimir Putin, the meeting also created useful propaganda. Now almost five years into a war he believed he would win in three days, he is coping with 1.5 million war casualties; the loss, as of this week, of half of his country’s oil-refining capacity; and even, in the past few days, the destruction of the Kerch Strait Bridge, which links Russia to Crimea. Putin built that bridge and personally attended the opening ceremony, treating it as a major national event. In recent days, the Ukrainians have struck the bridge three times, totally destroying the road link and at least temporarily halting rail traffic too. Nevertheless, Putin will use the Shenzhen meeting to tell Russians that their country is still a superpower, still allowed to sit in the same room as the Americans and the Chinese, still important on the world stage even as Russian power, influence, and prosperity dramatically shrink.

For Xi, the meeting was useful because he was the host, he set up the photographs, and his propaganda was broadcast around the world. With Trump’s cooperation, he telegraphed American decline, Chinese power, and Russian subservience.

Even as the Chinese economy is experiencing a real-estate slump, manufacturing losses, and chronic unemployment, he made China look like the only serious country in the room. The American president was babbling about airport greetings. Russia is bankrupt without Chinese support. But Xi, safe in the knowledge that he has successfully obtained the American chip technology his military and industry need, was the master of ceremonies.

Hidden inside this story of puffery and flattery is some good news. The leaders at the Yalta summit in 1945 really were able to decide the fate of smaller countries over their heads and against their wishes. The three leaders at Shenzhen don’t have that kind of power. Certainly the American president no longer has any cards, to use his own words, in Ukraine, which despite being cut off from all U.S. military and financial aid has continued fighting, with European backing and its own resources. Putin cannot dream of dominating European countries whose combined GDP is so much larger than his own country’s, and Xi is still far from being able to dominate Asia either.

The world has moved on since 1945—and even since 2022. When the Ukrainians struck the Kerch Bridge, they did so using their own weapons systems, none of which existed at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion. Over the past several months, the Iranians have been able to hit U.S. bases and targets in the Gulf States using Russian drone technology of equally recent vintage. We now live in a world of asymmetric conflicts, where even powers that claim to represent allegedly great civilizations are discovering that they can lose battles to much smaller ones. If the summit in Shenzhen looked anachronistic and obsolete—a failed attempt to re-create the glamour of the Cold War past—that’s because it was.

What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outages

Provided by UL Solutions

By Thomas Macaulay • 11.20.26

Hello!

Today: We explore the quest to make minds immortal, from head transplants and brain freezing to AI copies of ourselves. Plus: Trump has fired his cyber director after a wave of tech outages.

What we learned when our Roundtables went inside the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck.

Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”

Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”

It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”

There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”

To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

One more thing

The “steroid olympics” were a circus—and a window into our culture

—Amit Katwala

A couple of weeks ago, at a $50 million arena built in a casino parking lot in Las Vegas, I witnessed a libertarian thought experiment come to life. The inaugural Enhanced Games were the first sporting competition where participants were encouraged to take performance-enhancing drugs.

For the event’s supporters, the Enhanced Games offered a glimpse of a future where medical advances push the human race to new heights—and they never have to get old. As I watched the games unfold, two questions bounced around my head: Were they right? And what does that mean for the rest of us?

Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding (4 minute read)

Apple is developing an autonomous AI agent that can get things done on behalf of users similar to offerings by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others. The company is currently seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant that can write code, browse the web, control apps, and navigate devices on a user's behalf. Apple is working on agents that can plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs while coordinating specialized subagents along the way. The company's App Store has been dominated by AI agents, so it has introduced a new warning in the upcoming macOS 27.3 update that prompts users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

Science & Futuristic Technology

Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains (4 minute read)

Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029. Google's Project Suncatcher program is a long-term moonshot that aims to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into solar power. Its satellites each have the computing capacity of roughly the scale of a data center rack. The mission on New Glenn will deploy satellites into a Sun-synchronous orbit, where they will be able to receive nearly continuous solar energy.

Spacecraft reaches Mercury on second-ever mission to enter its orbit (4 minute read)

The BepiColombo mission is now preparing to swing into orbit around Mercury. The joint European-Japanese space mission aims to help scientists understand how Mercury formed so close to the Sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what makes up the frozen ice under the planet's permanently shadowed craters. The spacecraft will separate into two orbiters in early December. The orbiters will maneuver to different polar orbits around the planet, and science operations will begin in April next year.

The most important number in AI (42 minute read)

The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is a measure of AI progress developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization. It provides a single number that summarizes how well AI models do on benchmarks. It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. This post covers how the ECI is constructed, the challenges of benchmark selection, whether it makes sense to talk about 'model IQ', whether static benchmarks stay relevant as models get better, and much more.

AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. UKRAINE. RUSSIA. Sausage making

Trump puts allies through the grinder and on the menu.

Ukraine’s European allies met in Berlin Thursday as Donald Trump heralded his meeting with Xi Jinping and “friend” Vladimir Putin in China. Friedrich Merz said “a ‘Yalta’ format won’t bring peace.” Putin asked, “What was bad about Yalta?”

INTELLIGENCE. The Shenzhen trilateral was more a photo-op than a repeat of Yalta, which carved up Europe in 1945, but as far as Kyiv is concerned, the omens are ominous. Ukraine, not nuclear arms control, appears to have been the main topic. And while Trump has not overtly taken Russia’s side in the war, he’s given it moral equivalence, plus a reason to fight on, despite the costs, ruling out a Black Sea truce as Ukraine again struck the Kerch bridge to Crimea.

FOR BUSINESS. As Trump pressures Brussels and Kyiv to concede to Putin’s demands, he not only emboldens Moscow but damages the trust of others who might have once sought US intercession against Russia or China. From the Caucasus to Taiwan, the US will be seen less as a neutral arbiter than a potential camp follower for whoever it perceives to be the winning side. And even if it delivers a quick win, the approach undermines the logic of US alliance.

Welcome, humans.

So apparently Nvidia is in advanced talks to buy a startup called Inception for at least $500M, per The Information. Nothing is confirmed, and Inception is shutting down its API on December 28 anyway. The shutdown notice never mentions a buyer. It just has a countdown.

Here's why anyone cares. Most chatbots write one token (a word or chunk of a word) at a time, and each one depends on the last. Inception's Mercury models are diffusion models, which work on a whole block of text at once and refine it over several passes. Think of an editor fixing three paragraphs in the same sitting instead of typing line by line. Corey's takeaway from talking to cofounder Stefano Ermon is that this squeezes more useful output from the same GPU work. Which is a very nice pitch to make to a company that sells GPUs.

Mercury 3 reportedly runs at 1,068 tokens per second on Nvidia hardware, and Corey's eight API tests cost about four cents total. Results were uneven, though. It built a working dungeon-crawler game that passed 2,000 randomized map checks, but fumbled some writing constraints. Our full breakdown has the details.

😸 Meta's AI agent Muse reportedly accessed Signal messages during internal testing

Meta's personal AI agent, Muse, is making its own employees nervous. Muse launched September 8 as an agent that can send emails, book travel, and make payments for you from a virtual machine in Meta's cloud.

Here's what Reuters reported:

Muse accessed Signal messages during internal testing.

Employees received unprompted responses that appeared to contain private information, including bank balances.

Meta said many apparent account mix-ups were hallucinations and called the incidents isolated.

Okay, so that hallucination defense is worth a second look. A hallucination is when an AI confidently makes something up, so a bank balance on screen could be invented instead of leaked. That means the reports don't establish the numbers belonged to real users. Either Muse leaked a real number or invented a convincing one. Pick your comfort level.

The Signal detail is the one to remember. Signal encrypts messages while they travel, so only the devices in the conversation can read them. But once your phone unscrambles a message, it's ordinary text on your screen. An agent with broad access to your device sits on that side of the lock. Encryption protects the road, not the destination. The coverage we could read doesn't say how Muse got in, but the principle holds.

Muse has faced this question before. In September, an Inc. columnist said Muse read his Mac's Messages database after he declined to grant access. Meta replied that the Mac integration is opt-in and needs both Full Disk Access (a Mac setting that lets an app read files anywhere on the computer) and a separate Messages connector.

Meta's position, then, is that permissions decide what Muse can reach.

🎓 AI Skill of the Day: Give your AI agent less access before its first task

An agent can only work with what it can reach, but broad access also puts private material in its path. So the size of a bad day depends on how much you handed over, not how smart the agent is. Here's the three-step habit for any agent that can operate your computer, after the Reuters Muse investigation.

Check what it can reach. List the apps, folders, and connected accounts the agent can open before you give it anything to do.

Start small. Pick a low-stakes task, like tidying one scratch folder, and give it the narrowest access the tool allows.

Review before it acts. Read the agent's proposed actions before it sends, purchases, or deletes anything.

Step three is the easiest to skip, so here's a prompt that makes it automatic.

Before you do anything, list every file, app, and account you plan to touch for this task. Wait for my approval before you send, buy, or delete anything.

A capable assistant still needs boundaries. Even the really smart interns don't get the company credit card on day one.

Welcome, curious minds

This is David, your decidedly human web crawler, and you're reading the Weekly Filet, the newsletter for curious minds who love it when something makes them go «Huh, I never thought of it this way!». Like every Friday, I'm here to help you make sense of what’s happening, and imagine what could be. It's great to have you.

You might want to give this a try: Weekly Filet TV, a new way to watch all the videos I've recommended since 2011.

Weekly Filet TV: lean back and watch the best of the web

Press play and watch 259 of the best videos Weekly Filet has recommended since 2011.

Weekly Filet •David Bauer

1. Climbing inside the machine

«Computers are magical, but they are not magic, and that's a really big distinction to raise kids on.» A wonderful talk by Linda Liukas, programmer, children's book author and playground designer, on engaging children with computers without the need for screens. «We don't learn French by only conjugating the irregular verbs or practising the grammar rules. We learn a language by speaking it, by singing it, by flirting in it, by immersing ourselves in it. And in a similar way, code is a language.»

Climbing inside the machine • Linda Liukas • GOTO Copenhagen 2026

2. Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law

There are good reasons for laws not changing too quickly. In a rapidly changing world, however, this slowness can be a problem. Enter: regulatory sandboxes, or Experimentierklauseln as the Germans apparently call them. «Experimental clauses» are temporary or scope-limited changes to laws, «to allow for real-time adaptation or alteration in response to changing threats, climate or technology.» A helpful primer.

Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law | NOEMA

Experiments with the rule of law around the world are creating the kind of resiliency we need in our era of uncertainty.…

European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in education Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/20/2026 - 11:30 Today, the European Commission and eight Member States are launching the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to pool resources and develop shared, secure and interoperable digital infrastructure and services for education. Getty Images © anyaberkut The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC. The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions. Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, together with Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education of the Netherlands, will welcome the launch. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: “Today's launch of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education is an important step towards achieving Europe's technological sovereignty in one of our most sensitive and strategic sectors. Education shapes our future, and Europe must be able to rely on trusted, safe and interoperable digital solutions that reflect European values and principles. By working together with the Member States, we can build a resilient European digital education infrastructure that supports learners, educators and schools across the Union.” Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness, said: “Recently, we officially launched the Education and Skills Package and announced the establishment of the EDU-EDIC consortium. Today, we are reiterating our commitment to reinforce education for Europe's future. Our priority is to ensure that education is ready for the AI era. We will work together with Member States to pool expertise in strategic areas such as cloud infrastructure, AI for education, secure data exchange across educational institutions, and Europe's education technology (Ed Tech) sector.” You can also about other European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC) Related topics Creating a digital society Digital skills Europe's Digital Decade European Digital Infrastructure Consortium Technological sovereignty Related content News article 20 November 2026 Member States join forces to develop sovereign digital infrastruc.

The Nvidia CEO scandal is impacting Asian American women in tech and academia. Here’s how. The reveal earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent. But what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media. “So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women,” said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people’s opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.” Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal will diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It’s a reminder that no accomplishments will completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes. Jensen Huang has since resigned However, the U.S. Justice Department has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy. “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” President Donald Trump told reporters this week. Asian women struggle to be taken seriously as leaders Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.” Depicting them like trophy wives “implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University. The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions. “I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. The legal standard that could help rein in AI

The legal standard that could help rein in AI. Some people have begun using the legal system to rein in AI companies and the harms they are creating. Cases are mounting. In October 2026, the parents of Bowen Wan sued Open AI, charging that its Chat GPT agent may have instructed their daughter to stop taking her medication, leading to her death In 2024, a mother sued the Character.AI company, claiming that its chatbot’s interactions with her son contributed to his suicide The state of Kentucky later filed suit , claiming that Character.AI’s software exposed minors to self-harm and psychological manipulation. Social media companies, powered by artificial intelligence, are also facing lawsuits about injuries they purportedly caused. Regulating AI was a hot issue during the 2026 midterms , too. Several candidates who won their races have a regulation agenda I am a former litigator and a professor of business law , and all this action signals to me that people are looking to the law to protect them from AI harm. But what is the legal liability of AI software? An answer may be found in a principle known as strict liability Applied properly, strict liability could restrain the risky parts of the AI industry and still allow it to provide the tools the public wants. Abnormally dangerous software Tort law protects people from negligence, such as who is responsible if you slip and fall in a store Strict liability is part of tort law, but it is used to hold a person or company responsible for harm even if they were not at fault, not negligent, or had no intent to create trouble. A 2026 lawsuit claims Chat GPT encouraged a young woman to stop taking her medication, leading to her death. Two types of strict liability matter for AI. One addresses abnormally dangerous activity , such as blasting with dynamite or transporting radioactive material. The other addresses when a product hurts someone using it AI programs likely fit the abnormally dangerous standard. The touchstone case was tried in the U.K. in 1868. In the decision, the court stated that if someone has “anything” under their power that is “likely to do mischief if it escapes, [he] must keep it in at his peril” and is “answerable for all the damage which is the natural consequence of its escape.” The defendant is liable even if they used “ the utmost care to prevent the harm .” An attorney could pursue this avenue if a company builds AI software that is supposed to stay in a sandbox—a place isolated from the rest of a computer or network—but loses control of it The AI industry’s recent admissions that the software creates all sorts of risks would make such cases stronger. When Anthropic filed for its initial public offering in October, numerous pages of the document detailed extraordinary risks that its frontier AI models could pose. One hitch in applying this type of strict liability is that an activity must not be in common usage Lawyers could make a strong case against so-call.

Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages

Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages. Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports: Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly. [. ] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's mac OS. of this story at Slashdot. .

California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China

California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China. California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued subpoenas to Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang regarding reports that they misled investors about advanced AI chips potentially reaching China. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a press release. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information -- and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The probe follows Huang's resignation amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy and comes as the SEC reportedly conducts a similar investigation. The Hill reports: Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta continued. [. ] Following the Huang scandal, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents Thursday showing the U.S. authorized the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told The Hill, "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." "Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," the spokesperson added. of this story at Slashdot. .
